plan.analysis: Record 0.8808 comes from the power-law seed; raising N 2000→20000 gave only +0.003, so the grid is not binding — the plateau shape and the weak random-block hill climber are. Since R ≈ plateau/(plateau+tail) for a flat-topped f*f, gains must come from a seed whose f*f drops faster, or from a much stronger local optimizer. Previous work: plain coarse-to-fine from the constant start only reached 0.806; power-law seed dominates. I bet on three distinct, cheap-to-test moves this generation: (1) scan genuinely different seed families (spike+bang-bang, two-sided beta singularities) that may put f*f closer to bang-bang; (2) a finite-difference L-BFGS ascent in log-height at coarse N then upsample; (3) a deterministic multiscale block-scaling sweep using FFT convolution so thousands of systematic moves fit in the budget.

experiments.hypothesis: The power-law seed is one point in a family; seeds whose f*f is closer to bang-bang (flat with a steeper right edge) have less tail mass for the same plateau and thus strictly higher R than 0.8808.
experiments.change: Keep the exact score function and the returned-best logic. At N=1200 build and score these seed families (exact R, no hill climb yet): (a) h_i=(i+0.5)^-a * (N-i-0.5)^-b for a,b in {0,0.25,0.5,0.75} (skip a=b=0, clamp exponents); (b) spike+bang-bang h_0=c, h_i=1 for i<M, h_i=1e-3 otherwise, c in {1,3,10,30,100}, M in {N/8,N/4,N/2,3N/4}; (c) power-law with a right-edge spike h_i=(i+0.5)^-0.5 + c*exp(-(N-1-i)/tau) for c in {0.5,2,10}, tau in {5,20,80}. Take the top 5 seeds by exact R, run 400 random log-domain block perturbations on each (same accept/keep-best rule), then take the overall best, upsample it to N=8000 and do 400 more perturbations. Print each family's best R and the final R. Return the best construction seen.

experiments.kind: finite-difference L-BFGS ascent in log-height, coarse-to-fine
experiments.hypothesis: The record's optimizer accepts only single random moves; a quasi-Newton method using finite-difference gradients of R in log-height coordinates at coarse N will find a better local optimum of the same shape, and upsampling plus a short climb will carry it above 0.8808.
experiments.change: Use scipy.optimize.minimize(method='L-BFGS-B', jac=None (2-point finite differences), bounds on u=log h in [-25,25]). Objective is -R with the exact scorer (use scipy.signal.fftconvolve instead of np.convolve for speed; same formula). Schedule by CPU time: first 40% of budget at N=120 from a resampled best start, next 30% at N=350 (upsample the best u by linear interpolation of h), final 30% at N=1200. After each stage, evaluate exact R, keep the global best h, and call keep_best. At the end upsample the best to N=20000 and run the original random block hill climb for whatever time remains, returning the best seen. Print each stage's N and R.
experiments.prediction: The stage-R sequence rises and the final returned R exceeds 0.8808 (gradient information finds a genuinely better shape than random blocks); if the coarse-R plateaus at ~0.87 upsampling may still not beat the record.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: switch to an exact adjoint/analytic gradient of R through the convolution (O(N log N) per step) and run full quasi-Newton at N=20000.
experiments.if_not: Conclude finite-difference gradients at coarse N lose too much resolution; keep the random climber but give it a systematically chosen move set instead.

experiments.kind: deterministic multiscale block-scaling sweep with FFT convolution
experiments.hypothesis: Random single blocks rarely improve a flat plateau; a deterministic sweep that tries a grid of scaling factors on every block at every scale will accumulate many small accepted improvements on the existing best shape and beat 0.8808.
experiments.change: Keep the exact score formula but implement it with scipy.signal.fftconvolve for speed (same L, S, T, M). Start from the resampled best construction at N=20000, u=log h. experiments.change: Replace p0012's random hillclimb with an exact-gradient L-BFGS-B ascent in u=log(h) at N=20000. Use scipy.signal.fftconvolve to compute L=conv(h,h) with the same zero padding as score. For fixed p compute M_p=(sum_j L_j^p)^(1/p), S=sum_j (L_j^2+L_j L_{j+1}+L_{j+1}^2)/3, T=sum h. Implement gradients: dS/dL_j=(L_{j-1}+4L_j+L_{j+1})/3 with zero outside; dM_p/dL_j=L_j^(p-1)/M_p^(p-1). Then dS/dh and dM_p/dh are obtained by convolving h with these L-space derivative arrays (the derivative of L_j=sum h_a h_{j-a} is 2h_{j-i}); chain to u by multiplying by h. Objective = S/(T^2 M_p). Warm-start L-BFGS-B through p=8,16,32,64, with u bounds [-30,30], using time.process_time() and stopping before a 2 s margin. After every p stage score the true h with score(h) and keep_best. Start from the provided best construction.

plan.analysis: p0017 showed the real lever: an exact N=200000 binomial (flat-half) seed jumps to 0.882542, which matches the continuous x^-1/2 value (||f*f||_inf=π/4, R=0.8825). The remaining loss is entirely the decaying tail of f*f after the plateau (tail L1 mass ≈0.215, tail L2 ≈0.076) — resolution and N=20000 polish are dead ends (F3, F10, F11). Since R=(plateauL2+tailL2)/(||g||_1·M), the only way up is to make f*f drop faster after x=1, i.e. reshape h near its right end so g's tail is narrower. I bet on right-edge shaping at N=200000 with exact FFT scoring, which is cheap (~0.03 s/eval) and allows hundreds of score evaluations. Interior low-frequency modulation is the control: if it does nothing, the flat-half interior is rigid and all effort belongs on the tail.

experiments.kind: tail-envelope optimization on high-N binomial seed
experiments.hypothesis: The R loss of the 0.882542 construction is only the f*f tail mass after the plateau. A smooth multiplicative envelope acting on the last ~40% of the binomial seed can steepen that tail (make f(1^-) decay so products near the truncation edge vanish sooner) without destroying plateau flatness, raising R.
experiments.change: Take start if given (length N, keep N; else build binomial h[k]=C(2k,k)/4^k at N=200000). First try start itself and keep it as best. Implement fast_score(h): L=scipy.signal.fftconvolve(h,h) (full linear conv, length 2N-1); pad conceptually with zeros; S=sum(L_j^2+L_j*L_{j+1}+L_{j+1}^2)/3 over consecutive pairs with the implicit zero end knots; T=h.sum()**2; M=L.max(); return S/(T*M). Sanity-check against helix_problem.score on 3 arrays (accept |diff|<1e-8 before using). Envelope: u=k/(N-1), w(u)=clip((u-u0)/(1-u0),0,1)^2 with u0=0.6, s(u)=w(u)*sum_{m=0}^{7} a_m u^m, h=binom*exp(s). Optimize a in R^8 by coordinate descent: init a=0; sweep m=0..7, try a_m +/- delta with delta init 0.06, accept only if fast_score improves; after a full sweep with no accept, delta*=0.5; also every ~50 sweeps try a random 3-coordinate simultaneous move. Stop when delta<2e-5 or time near deadline; keep global best; return best array (re-verified with helix score once).
experiments.prediction: Envelope optimization raises score by at least +0.0003 (>=0.8828), confirming the f*f tail can be sharpened and that its mass is the binding constraint.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: refine this with 16 envelope coefficients and a lower window start u0~0.4, plus a matching left-edge envelope; run at 60-90 s and combine with the best piecewise-decay tail found in the parallel experiment.
experiments.if_not: Conclude the x^-1/2 tail is already locally optimal under smooth smooth envelopes; abandon envelope fitting and pivot to a genuinely different f family (mixtures of two singular components, or a trimmed singularity with a cap), testing whether a longer plateau can be sustained.

experiments.hypothesis: The binomial's h stays ~k^-1/2 (slow decay) up to the last step, which is what makes f*f's tail long. experiments.change: Use the same fast_score as the envelope experiment (FFT conv). Start from start (length N; fallback binomial at N=200000); keep start as best if nothing beats it. Family: h_k = binom_k for k<=K; h_k = binom_K * ((N-1-k)/(N-1-K))^s for k>K. Grid K in {0.75,0.80,0.85,0.90,0.94,0.97}*(N-1), s in {0.5,1,2,4,8} (30 evals), keep the best. Return global best.
experiments.prediction: At least one (K,s) combo beats the pure binomial and refinement reaches >=0.8827, showing a forced sharper right edge helps; the best (K,s) tells where the plateau/tail trade-off sits (K close to N, s moderate).

experiments.if_not: Conclude that cutting the seed's right edge only hurts plateau flatness more than it helps the tail; drop right-edge truncation and test resculpting via added mass (a second small component) instead.

experiments.change: Use fast_score (FFT conv, same as above). plan.analysis: The record has sat exactly at 0.882542 for a full generation: every right-edge envelope, forced taper, interior cosine mode and global tilt returned the start unchanged. The p0017 binomial (h_k=C(2k,k)/4^k) makes f*f exactly flat on the first half, so all remaining loss lives in the tail after x=1 and in the fact that we are at a strong local maximum for coordinate-style moves. The three bets this generation are structurally different from that saturated family: (1) superpose shifted copies of the seed, which by associativity produces overlapping plateaus with controlled offset (a genuinely new g, not an envelope); (2) a projected analytic-gradient ascent on R itself at full N with the hard max (the earlier L-BFGS used a softmax at N=20000, which may have hidden the real directions); (3) inverse design: fix a trapezoid target g with tunable ramp width, deconvolve for h by projected gradient, and measure the best attainable R — this tells us whether a flatter-than-current g is reachable at all.

experiments.hypothesis: f*f = (u*u)*(delta0+lam*delta_s)^2, so superposing a shifted copy of the binomial on itself builds f*f out of overlapping flat plateaus offset by s; for s a moderate fraction of N the outer ramps may be narrower relative to the plateau than the single x^-1/2 tail, raising R.
experiments.change: Reuse p0020's fast_score (it is already sanity-checked against helix score) and take N and h0 = start (fallback: binomial h[k]=h[k-1]*(2k-1)/(2k), h[0]=1, N=200000). Scan s in {N//200, N//50, N//20, N//10, N//5, 3N//10, N//2} and lam in {0.1,0.25,0.5,1.0,2.0}: h[k]=h0[k]+lam*h0[k-s] for k>=s, h0[k] otherwise; evaluate fast_score, track the best. Also test the 3-copy variant h0+lam*shift(h0,s)+lam*shift(h0,2s) at the best few (s,lam). Then coordinate-descend on lam in [0.01,10] and integer s within +-N//200 of the best, re-scoring with fast_score, and every new best must be re-verified with the exact helix score and stored via keep_best. Spend any leftover time on random log-domain block perturbations biased to the last 20% of indices, accepting only improvements, always keeping the global best. Leave 1 s margin.
experiments.prediction: Most (s,lam) combinations drop R below 0.88 sharply; the experiment is informative either way: if some s~N/10..3N/10 with lam~1 gives >0.883, plateau extension by superposition works; if the best stays within 1e-5 of 0.882542, the single x^-1/2 seed is essentially the whole story and mixtures are refuted.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: fine-grid s and lam around the winner, add a third independent-shift coefficient and a per-copy amplitude (3-4 parameters), and jointly polish the outer tails; also test the same superposition on a symmetrized seed.
experiments.if_not: Drop superposition; treat the one-block x^-1/2 seed as fixed and rely on the gradient and inverse-design experiments for shape freedom, pivoting to changing the objective/target rather than the seed mixture.

experiments.kind: analytic-gradient projected ascent on R (hard max, full N)
experiments.hypothesis: The coordinate/block climbers and the softmax L-BFGS-B ascent only explored smoothed or single-coordinate moves and stalled; the exact gradient of R=(S/(T*M)) at full N, using the true argmax for M, can point in joint directions (whole plateau + tail) that no local move found, so a projected ascent can still raise R above 0.882542.
experiments.change: Take N and h=start (fallback binomial, N=200000). Implement exact R and its analytic gradient exactly as follows, verified against helix score on 3 test arrays before use: L=fftconvolve(h,h); S=sum(L_j^2+L_j L_{j+1}+L_{j+1}^2)/3 plus the two implicit-zero end pairs; T=(sum h)^2; M=L.max(), j*=argmax(L). dS/dL_j = (2L_j+L_{j-1}+L_{j+1})/3 (neighbors zero outside). Adjoint to h: gS = corr(c,h)+conv(c,h) with c=dS/dL, i.e. gS[i]=sum_j c_j (h[j-i]+h[i-j]) implemented with fftconvolve(c, h[::-1]) and fftconvolve(c, h) and correct slicing; gT = 2*(sum h)*ones; gM[i] = h[abs-of j*-i] pair as above from the single argmax. gradR = (gS*T*M - S*(gT*M + T*gM))/(T*M)^2. Ascend: h <- maximum(0, h + step*gradR/||gradR||), with backtracking line search (halve step until exact R increases), re-picking the argmax each iteration; reset step when stalled. Run until close to the deadline, keep_best on every exact-R improvement, leave 1 s margin. Optionally every 200 iterations restart step at a larger value to escape flat regions.
experiments.prediction: Either it finds an ascent direction and reaches >=0.8827 within 40 s (showing the random climbers left real slack and the exact hard-max gradient matters at full N), or ||gradR|| directions all fail line search and the score stays within 1e-6 of 0.882542 for the whole run, confirming a strong local maximum of R under the full gradient.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: run many more gradient steps with momentum/Adam and a smoothed-but-tight max, then hand the result to the coordinate climber; also try the gradient on a 2-component parametrization.
experiments.if_not: Conclude the shape is a gradient-stationary point; abandon direct ascent on R and shift all budget to inverse design / target reshaping and to the superposition family, and consider a coarser (N=20000) but fully global optimizer whose result is then upsampled to N=200000.

experiments.kind: inverse design via deconvolution toward a trapezoid target
experiments.hypothesis: Rather than reshaping the current g, ask which flat-top g (trapezoid with tunable ramp width r) is actually attainable as an autoconvolution: minimizing ||h*h - alpha*g||^2 by projected gradient from the binomial gives, for each r, the best f producing that plateau shape, and measuring R of the result reveals whether a sharper-ramped g than the current tail can be realized.
experiments.change: Take N and h0=start (fallback binomial, N=200000). Build target arrays g_r of length 2N-1 equal to 1 on j in [r, 2N-1-r] and linear ramps of width r at each end (0 outside), for r in {200, 1000, 5000, 20000}; also center the plateau at the same midpoint as h0's plateau. For each r run ~150 iterations of projected gradient on F(h)=||h*h - alpha*g||^2 with h>=0: compute L=fftconvolve(h,h), residual d=L-alpha*g, adjoint gradient grad[i]=sum_j d_j (h[j-i]+h[i-j]) via fftconvolve(d,h[::-1])+fftconvolve(d,h) with correct slicing, step with backtracking line search on F, alpha updated in closed form alpha=(L.g)/(g.g) each iteration. After each r's run, evaluate exact R(h), keep_best, and give the best two results a short coordinate/log polish. Record and print R for every r. Leave 1 s margin.
experiments.prediction: Small r (sharp ramps) will fit poorly and give R well below 0.8825; r near the current tail's effective width should reproduce ~0.8825; if any r yields R>0.883 the experiment identifies a better plateau shape to chase, while uniform R<=0.8825 across all r shows the current trapezoid-ish g is essentially the attainable optimum and that the loss is intrinsic to autoconvolution admissibility rather than to our search.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: replace the trapezoid by a free monotone-knot target (8-10 knots) and repeat the deconvolution, then polish the resulting f directly on R; this becomes the new seed family.
experiments.if_not: Conclude the target family adds nothing; next generation spend the budget on the mixture/three-copy family with more parameters and on direct R-gradient with momentum, and test whether N larger than 200000 (if allowed) or a different discretization of the singular endpoint changes the constant.

plan.analysis: The record 0.882542 has been frozen for three generations. Every local move — envelopes, tapers, cosine modes, tilts, superposition, exact-gradient ascent, deconvolution toward trapezoid targets — returns the start unchanged. That is strong evidence the binomial construction is a genuine local maximum for shape-preserving moves, and that the real ceiling is the continuous x^-1/2 value (~0.8825 with ||f*f||_inf=π/4). To beat it we need a structurally different f, not a reshaped binomial. Two untried directions: (1) a genuinely different seed family — asymmetric two-sided power laws with independent left/right exponents and a spike, which produce a different f*f plateau shape; (2) a coarse-resolution free-form optimization (N~2000-5000) that can escape the binomial basin because the landscape is smoother and cheaper, then upsample and polish. I bet on the coarse free-form search as the most likely to find a new basin.

experiments.hypothesis: At N=2000-5000 the R landscape is smooth enough that a multi-start random/structured hill climb can find basins the N=200000 binomial polish cannot reach; upsampling a coarse optimum to N=200000 and polishing may exceed 0.882542.
experiments.change: Ignore start. Set N=3000. Run 6 independent restarts, each: seed h_i = (i+0.5)^-0.5 * (1 + 0.3*randn) (log-normal jitter), then log-domain block hill climb (block sizes N//20, N//100, single) with adaptive eps in [0.005,0.05], accepting only improvements, for ~5 s each. Keep the best coarse h. Then upsample to N=200000 by linear interpolation, and run a short log-domain polish (block N//500 biased to tail, single-coordinate, eps 0.02) for the remaining time. Return the best full-resolution array. Use fast fftconvolve scorer.

plan.analysis: The record has been frozen at 0.882542 for three generations. Every local full-N move (random block coordinate, envelopes, tapers, tilted masses, superposition, analytic gradient, trapezoid deconvolution) returns the start literally unchanged, so the binomial is a genuine stationary/rigid point for those movers, and the loss is entirely the post-plateau tail of f*f. Coarse free-form search (0.8521) and asymmetric power laws (0.486) are dead ends. Betting that the remaining slack requires (a) a parametric family with an explicit right-end decay exponent — a coherent, low-dimensional change rather than hundreds of random coordinates — and (b) coherent global deformations of log h (Gaussian smoothing of the singular endpoint, and a multi-mode Fourier envelope optimized jointly). These are the kinds of moves not yet tried at full resolution.

experiments.kind: parametric endpoint-exponent family (s+eps)^-1/2 (1-s)^b exp(a s) with derivative-free optimization
experiments.hypothesis: The x^-1/2 seed makes f*f exactly flat on [0,1] but leaves a long algebraic tail because h does not decay at the right end and the singularity at 0 is unregularized. Adding a right-end vanishing factor (1-s)^b and a shift eps of the singular point trades a little plateau flatness for a much shorter tail; a coherent 3-parameter family can capture this trade-off where random block moves cannot.
experiments.change: Ignore start. N=200000. Build h_i = (s_i+eps)^-1/2 * max(1-s_i,1e-12)^b * exp(a*s_i) with s_i=(i+0.5)/N, clipped to [1e-12, inf). Score exactly with fftconvolve and the L-knot formula. First evaluate a grid: eps in {0,1e-3,1e-2,5e-2}, b in {0,0.1,0.25,0.5}, a in {0,0.5,1.0} (eps=0,b=0,a=0 is the plain binomial, guaranteeing >=0.882542). Then run scipy.optimize.minimize with method='Nelder-Mead' on -score in (eps,b,a), starting from the best grid point and 2 runners-up, for the remaining time; keep the best h found. Return it.
experiments.prediction: Grid + Nelder-Mead returns the plain binomial (0.882542) if no family member helps, or a score above 0.882542 (by >1e-5) if a small right-end decay + shift shortens the tail profitably.
experiments.if_gain: Expand the family: add (1-s)^b with b allowed negative near the left end, add a second scale exp(-c s^2), and re-optimize with more Nelder-Mead restarts at N=200000.
experiments.if_not: Conclude the x^-1/2 plateau is optimal within smooth endpoint-modulated families; abandon parametric seeds and rely on coherent global deformations of the full array.

experiments.kind: global Gaussian smoothing of log-heights (coherent deformation scan)
experiments.hypothesis: Random block moves fail because they destroy the plateau locally. A single coherent operation — convolving log h with a Gaussian kernel of width r — changes h smoothly at all scales at once. Modest r regularizes the singular left endpoint and softens the right end, potentially shortening the f*f tail while keeping the plateau nearly flat.
experiments.change: Take start (the 0.882542 construction), N=200000. Compute g0=log(max(start,1e-12)). For r in {1e-4,3e-4,1e-3,3e-3,1e-2,3e-2}: build normalized Gaussian kernel of index-width sigma=max(1,round(r*N)), padded/truncated at 4 sigma, convolve g0 (mode='same', edge-padded) to get gs. For lam in {0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.85,1.0}: h=exp((1-lam)*g0+lam*gs), score exactly; keep best. Then refine around the best (r,lam) pair with a finer local grid (lam +-0.1 step 0.02, r multiplied by {0.5,0.75,1.5,2}) for the remaining time. Keep global best.
experiments.prediction: If coherent smoothing shortens the tail more than it flattens the plateau, one (r,lam) beats 0.882542; if not, best stays exactly 0.882542, confirming coherence alone is not the missing ingredient.
experiments.if_gain: Replace the fixed Gaussian with a free smooth multiplier kernel of 8-12 knots in index space and optimize its values by coordinate descent, then polish.
experiments.if_not: Conclude the construction is stable under smooth coherent deformations; stop mutating the binomial and spend all future budget on genuinely different constructions (e.g. inverse-designed smooth flat-top targets).

experiments.kind: multi-mode global Fourier envelope optimization (joint 6-mode coordinate descent)
experiments.hypothesis: The previous single-mode cosine scan tested modes one at a time and only small amplitudes; a joint envelope with several modes can produce a coherent reshape that no single mode achieves (e.g. simultaneously lifting the mid-support and suppressing the right end). If the binomial is rigid even to this, the case for a structurally different f is settled.
experiments.change: Take start. N=200000, x_i=i/N, g0=log(max(start,1e-12)). Model log h = g0 + sum_{m=1..6} c_m cos(pi*m*x) + c_0 (constant is irrelevant, skip). Coordinate descent: c=zeros(6); repeat sweeps of m=1..6, for each m try step values {+-0.1,+-0.05,+-0.02,+-0.01,+-0.005} of c_m, keep any that raises the exact score; after each full sweep halve the step set; run 4 sweeps or until 22 s elapsed. Keep global best h and return it.
experiments.prediction: Either some joint envelope exceeds 0.882542 (proving global interior slack exists and pointing where), or the best remains 0.882542 through all sweeps.
experiments.if_gain: Take the winning envelope, force it to zero at the right end, re-optimize jointly with the tail exponent parameters from the parametric experiment, and polish at N=200000.
experiments.if_not: Report the binomial construction as rigid to all coherent global modulations; next generation starts a fundamentally different construction (smooth flat-top super-Gaussian target inverse design or a two-scale mixture designed to lengthen the plateau beyond 1/2).
